segments.text: Joining me is V. Anant Nageswaran, Chief Economic Advisor to Government of India.
Sir, welcome.
You work closely with the Prime Minister.
You're a part of this journey, Viksit Bharat by 2047.
As India emerges as the fastest growing major economy, in your view, sir, how much of this is the reforms he initiated?
What do you make of this journey so far?
Thank you for having me on your show.
I mean, to answer your question, I would say a very, very high proportion of the credit to India's journey towards becoming a Vixit Bharat and the fact that many Indians are even able to
aspire for and dream of that possibility owes a lot to the kind of economic stewardship that the honorable prime minister has provided in the last 12 years.
He inherited an economy that was partly or largely broken because we had a high current account deficit
We had double-digit inflation rates and we had a currency that had just cratered and fiscal deficit was very high and the banking system was in a crisis and so were corporate balance sheets.
We should not forget that these were the legacy that he inherited on the macroeconomic front.

So given that to have repaired the bank balance sheets and today Indian banks non-performing assets are at a historical low and the insolvency and bankruptcy code also helped corporate balance sheets to become healthy and then he unleashed financial inclusion to the PM Jandan Yojana

and then handled COVID so well compared to many other nations that India was able to recover and bounce back with very high growth rates in 2021-22 and 2022-23 and sustain them in the following three years as well.
And I'm leaving out an important landmark reform, single nation, single tax, the goods and services tax, apart from the fact that from 2017-18,
Public investment in infrastructure and capital expenditure had gone up by three and a half to four X four times.

And so much so that India's infrastructure when it comes to airports, road connectivity, energy generation, the number of metro cities that have metro rail and the inland water transport for free, etc.
If you really look at them, these have lifted India's potential growth rate.
And it also lifted India's aspirations and all the while maintaining macroeconomic stability, having inherited a very high fiscal deficit and with the COVID compounding it, he has fixed it.
India earned its first credit rating upgrade in 2025.
So we can go on.
So clearly, it's interesting you point out, sir, that from fragile five, he was in 2013 14.
He's been able to bring it to the fastest growing large economy right now.
But the challenges, you know,

that were en route and we'll talk about those in a moment but the challenge is right now there are many who says jobs for example or private investment for example that's yet to pick up at the full scale in your view sir what's holding that back what more needs to be done to unlock that animal instinct or that potential
No, you are right, the private corporate sector.
But first of all, let me tell you that India's overall capital formation rate at 33%, 34% of GDP is a very high number.
So there is capital formation happening.
And you can say that it is because of public investment by government and the state governments as well, given the 50-year interest-free loans.
And within the private sector, I think there are some research reports that show that
listed companies have been doing better than non-listed companies or unlisted companies when it comes to capital formation.
But the biggest reason that you are looking at a much higher number but it is not there are multiple.
One is the global uncertainty, the kind of extraordinarily high degree of manufacturing competition coming from China given their own deflation, given their own domestic economy travails

They rely extremely heavily on exports and their deflation is making them utilize the global markets, which naturally makes investors in other countries pull back and decide when to put their money to work, et cetera.
But having said that, India's capital formation in the private sector is beginning to rise in the last few quarters.
And the bank credit growth to industry is running at 20%.

And I think given the kind of steady growth rate that we have witnessed in the Indian economy, the private sector capital formation, and I hear I refer to the unlisted space, I think it will catch up with the households and with the public sector.
In fact, making them step back a bit and private sector capital formation will probably take over the baton from these two segments of the economy.
Back to you.
Sir, you spoke of the global headwinds.
You know, you spoke of COVID-19.
So 2020, that was a huge challenge.
Then 2022, the Russia-Ukraine war, both energy and fertilizers, adversely impacted.
Then again 2025 and 2026, you've had Iran, US and Israel conflict, the impact again on energy and fertilizers.
What's it like working with the Prime Minister when these challenges come and you sit in the Prime Minister's office and talk about how do you overcome these challenges?
Of course, I mean, I don't sit in the Prime Minister's office.
The Chief Economic Adviser's office is part of the Ministry of Finance, but I do.
do regular periodic updates on the macro situation to the Honorable Prime Minister.

I think one of the things that you alluded to in your own initial intro remarks is his laser-like focus and his ability to remember details and to ensure follow-up and a steady hand, at the same time not losing focus on the underlying inherent strengths of the economy
for meeting short-term needs.
He doesn't sacrifice the long-term macroeconomic stability or financial prudence.

Even if the short-term situation calls for remedies, he's able to keep an eye on the medium-term strings that have been serving Indian economy very well over the last 12 years, even as he has to take short-term measures to make sure that the economy is able to handle the crisis.
We saw that in the pandemic.

We saw that during the 2022 Russia-Ukraine crisis, and even this year in ensuring supply of cooking gas, natural gas, crude oil, diversifying the sources, using the crisis to make people move from cooking gas to pipe, natural gas, et cetera.
And then in the last two years, you have seen the liberalization of nuclear energy.
The draft rules have been announced recently and also launching
the critical minerals and earth's mission.
So it is the ability to manage the short-term crisis and the exigency while keeping a very firm and clear-eyed focus on the medium to long-term priorities I would say are his core strengths.

Okay and you know you've talked of GDP growth numbers they remain strong 7.8 percent even though there was a storm in a teacup or more politically over certain numbers but if we were to come to rural income for example or wages you know which would give you that sense that
as India grows that journey towards Viksit Bharat, salaries are also going up.
Now, that also remains under pressure.
Now, what more needs to be done and what is the Prime Minister and your entire team, you know, the finance minister, you, the entire team doing to ensure that growth should be felt across sectors.
Yeah.
Absolutely, undoubtedly.
I mean, economic growth per se would count for very little unless it touches people's lives and makes a difference.
There should be no doubt about that.
And rural income and rural employment growth, if you look at the annual numbers, they have been steadily improving post-COVID.
In fact, it is the recent monthly data that have been somewhat cyclically

Drifting lower but annual numbers show a very robust growth in both the rural employment and incomes clearly rural income growth the cyclical in nature and this year's monsoon has introduced a certain sense of uncertainty.

With respect to agricultural output and rural demand down the road so government will be very much alive to the situation and responding to that, if necessary, but to your broader question about what we should be doing and for the government has been doing a lot I think memories are a bit short these days.
because of the onslaught of information from social media.

But July 2024 budget by the government was exclusively focused on employment, whether it is corporate internship, apprenticeship schemes, incentives for first-time jobs created by companies in manufacturing and in non-manufacturing sectors, contributing to some of the provident fund contributions by the employees, the government taking over the employer's contribution so that
They don't feel disincentivized to hire because of pension contributions which the government took over.
So the entire July 2024 budget was about employment generation.
Second, the labor intensive free trade agreements that the government is now signing.
With the UK, it is now active, and with the European Union it is going to become active by the end of the year.
And these agreements open labor intensive goods and services sectors for Indian producers and entrepreneurs.

The third thing that the government is doing, it is actively facilitating deregulation efforts in states, and that is an effort underway both in the union government of course that is separate, but in the states as well where there is a touch point of the local governments with the businesses, small businesses.
And this deregulation will lower the cost of doing business for small and medium businesses in states and therefore contributing to their hiring much more.
So I would say fiscal initiatives, free trade agreements,
deregulation initiatives and the various incentives given for capital formation by the state's 50-year interest-free loans and ensuring that credit availability to MSMEs.
Look at the MSME credit code from the banking sector.
It is running at nearly 23%.

So all these things and then the various initiatives given for startups and new businesses etc all of these things given the uncertainties despite the global uncertainties all of these things are contributing to keeping up job creation all will continue to facilitate job creation in the Indian economy in the coming years.
and manufacturing.
That's been one of the key focus areas and key result areas for the Prime Minister.
We've heard him talk about Atmanirbhar Bharat, increased manufacturing on ground.
I mean, considering China manufactures so much that it's exporting finished products, on ground, how much of our manufacturing is actually taking off?
What more needs to be done to ensure that our manufacturing is world-class, competitive,
export-oriented too.
I mean, the entire PLI initiative is all about bringing manufacturing to a greater share of gross value addition, GVA, in the economy.
And in fact, in constant prices, India's manufacturing share of GVA has been rising from 14% something to 16.1% in the last three years in constant price terms.

And I think apart from the PLI initiatives, ensuring energy availability, ensuring skilling, creating these free trade agreements so that manufacturing can export goods with lower or no duties, et cetera, and also reducing the customs duties on intermediate goods and inputs, which were the major plans of the budget announced in February, 2026.
and then creating demand visibility for manufactured goods in the country through reduction in direct taxes and indirect taxes in the course of 2025.
All these are all measures to ensure that Indian businesses continue to grow their manufacturing share
because free trade agreements bring in the element of competition as well and then also induce businesses to invest in R&D.
So multiple measures are underway and the manufacturing share of GBA rising is showing that these efforts are bearing fruit.

And how would you describe you know Prime Minister Narendra Modi's personal role in shaping the economic policies in the past 12 years and of course the road ahead because 4 trillion dollars to reach that 30 trillion dollar mark by 2047 this will have to grow a multi-fold and manifold now sir.
To describe his personal goal is to simply say that he is the architect of the economic policy.
He is the architect of the manufacturing vision and of the world class infrastructure that India has been creating over the last 12 years.

And also, he is the one who anticipated the supply chain disruptions and weaponization that could happen, and which is why he called for Atman-Irbarta and indigenization since the Russia-Ukraine war broke out.
And I think his emphasis on indigenization is turning out to be prescient.
even that more and more supply chain choke points and weaponization is emerging increasingly so in the world.

And then when you look at the fiscal prudence and fiscal stability, which has brought down the overall interest rates in the Indian economy, even though it has gone up in the last few weeks or so, the 10-year bond yield at 7% from India is at historical lows, which is what brought us the
credit rating upgrade as well, even as it improved the quality of fiscal expenditure by increasing the capital expenditure share and lowering the revenue expenditure share.

All of these things are, he is the architect of all these policies, whether it is financial inclusion, Jan Dhan Yojana and the mobile phone and the Jam Trinity, digital public infrastructure, we all know that
He is a big believer in the role of technology in improving lives and improving efficiency in the economy.
So I would say his imprint is very evident in almost every major policy initiative and the macroeconomic stability that have underpinned India's rise amidst massively rising global uncertainties.
So that is why we are confident that while there are challenges,
because we are a lower middle income economy right now.
There are challenges about in geopolitics, in climate change, in supply chain, etc.
We are confident that we can meet these challenges because he has focus, he has determination, and he has vision and the passion to deliver on India's Viksit Bharat aspirations.

Sir, for joining me here on this India First special broadcast because that vision and that dream of a vikasit Bharat by 2047, you know, that's actually a nation's dream to be a developed country and that inclusive development.
Many thanks for joining me and hope to have you on India First more often.
Many thanks, sir.
Welcome.
